doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Life in the Mott Haven projects and the Fleet family neighbors
summary: Vega describes the projects as a step up from the tenements, the mixed community, and neighbors including Biddy Fleet's family and a cop named Carl.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. That’s how it was when I was growing up. And mind you we were in the Mott Haven which is one of the poorest parts of the poorest Congressional district in the United States. But when we were coming up the parents, the parents that moved their families into the projects, the projects were the next step up from living in the tenements. But one of our neighbors, which I didn’t find out until many, many years later, one of our neighbors was the Fleet family. And I always knew the Fleet family, you know they were all well-dressed people, and then it wasn’t until I was living in Vermont and I made mention on social media that I was speaking to my jazz history class about Biddy Fleet, who was the guitarist that worked with Charlie Parker and then the son James Fleet contacts me and he tells me, “Ray, I’ve never told you this but that’s my father.” And he was living in the projects with us. They were living in the projects. I think Biddy wanted to continue — I think he continued a job as some kind of a social — he had like a government job, usually postal work probably, something to that effect. But that’s what stopped him from going on the road and continuing playing music full time. But the son, James, I went to high school with, he went to elementary school, middle school, and high school with my brother Julio. All the grades. And he’s a visual artist like my brother, but he also plays saxophone. But these were the types of families that were living in the projects at the time. They were, the projects were supposed to be a step up from the tenements of Harlem, the tenements of places like Williamsburg, Brooklyn or where my parents moved in from which was in East Harlem which they called The Barrio. So moving to the projects was like a big, big move up. Plus my building had 13 floors or has — the building’s still there — has 13 floors and eight apartments per floor. And I could tell you that as a kid growing up I could probably identify every family in the building. We all knew each other. And people looked out for each other. And it was a hodgepodge of — there was people from African-American background, people whose families came up during the great migration of the latter part of the teens of the twentieth century, there were folks that came in from Puerto Rico, some folks from the Dominican Republic, folks from the Caribbean like Jamaica. I remember there was a white family that lived upstairs and he was a cop. His name was Carl and we knew him. We knew him, he was a cop, he was a cop. He was a beat cop, he had his uniform, and he was living in the projects. So you know a lot of times people think, oh the cops are not going to lift — no
this guy Carl lived in the projects and we all knew him and the kids went to school in our neighborhood. It’s interesting.
